chapter_summary:
Networking turns a Raspberry Pi from a standalone computer into a connected device. The Raspberry Pi 3, 4, and 5, as well as the Zero W and Zero 2 W, have built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The Pi 4 and Pi 5 also have a Gigabit Ethernet port for wired networking. Wired connections are usually faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi, so use Ethernet when possible for servers or long-running projects.

To check your network connection, use the `ip` command:

```bash
ip a
```

This shows all network interfaces and their IP addresses. The wired interface is usually called `eth0`, and the wireless interface is usually called `wlan0`. An IP address looks like `192.168.1.45` and is assigned by your router through DHCP.

You can test connectivity with the `ping` command:

```bash
ping google.com
```

`ping` sends small packets to a remote server and prints the response time. Press Ctrl+C to stop it. If `ping` works, your Pi has internet access.

For headless access, SSH is the most common tool. SSH stands for Secure Shell and provides an encrypted command-line connection over the network. On another computer, open a terminal and run:

```bash
ssh alex@raspberrypi.local
```

If the Pi and your computer are on the same local network, the `.local` hostname usually works thanks to mDNS, also called Bonjour or Avahi. If not, use the Pi's IP address.

To copy files to or from the Pi, use `scp`:

```bash
scp notes.txt alex@raspberrypi.local:/home/alex/
scp alex@raspberrypi.local:/home/alex/data.csv ./
```

For larger transfers or directories, `rsync` is more efficient because it only copies changed files:

```bash
rsync -avz projects/ alex@raspberrypi.local:/home/alex/projects/
```

For graphical remote access, enable VNC through `raspi-config` or the Raspberry Pi Configuration GUI. Then install RealVNC Viewer on your main computer and connect to the Pi's IP address or hostname. VNC is useful when you need to use graphical applications or help someone troubleshoot a desktop issue.

Security matters when a device is networked. Here are basic practices:

- Change the default password and use a strong, unique password.
- Disable password-based SSH and use SSH keys instead for stronger authentication.
- Keep Raspberry Pi OS updated with `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`.
- Disable services you do not need.
- Avoid exposing SSH directly to the public internet without additional protection such as a firewall or VPN.

screens.title: Networking, SSH, and VNC
screens.subtitle: Make your Raspberry Pi reachable, manageable, and secure on your local network

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to make a Raspberry Pi join and use a network, how to find and confirm its network address, and how to access it remotely both by a secure command line and by a graphical desktop. We’ll cover wired and wireless options, the basic commands that reveal your IP address and connectivity, and practical tools for remote access like secure shell and remote desktop. You will also see how to copy files safely and keep your device secure when it is on the network. For example, a headless Pi acting as a small server benefits from Ethernet for reliability, while a portable Pi Zero W is most convenient on Wi‑Fi. A common mistake is assuming the Pi’s hostname will always resolve; sometimes you must use the numerical IP address. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to find the Pi’s address, open a secure shell session, move files with efficient tools, and enable a graphical link for troubleshooting — all while applying simple security steps to reduce risk. Consider: which method will you use for an always‑on server versus a temporary demo?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Network access plus secure remote tools turn a Pi into a manageable, networked computer — use Ethernet for reliability, SSH for secure shell access, scp/rsync for file transfer, and VNC for graphical needs.

screens.title: Wired vs Wireless on the Pi
screens.subtitle: When to choose Ethernet or Wi‑Fi and what each provides

narration.text: Choosing between wired Ethernet and Wi‑Fi depends on reliability, speed, and the intended role of the Pi. Ethernet provides a consistent connection and is recommended for servers and long‑running projects because it is less sensitive to interference and offers full duplex Gigabit bandwidth on Pi 4 and Pi 5 models. Wireless is convenient for portable Pis such as the Zero W series and for temporary setups; built‑in Wi‑Fi makes field experiments and demos simple. Keep in mind that the interfaces are named in the operating system — typically eth0 for wired and wlan0 for wireless — and that most home networks use DHCP to assign an IP address automatically. A common misconception is that Wi‑Fi is always slower; that depends on the Wi‑Fi standard, signal strength, and network congestion. For example, running a small web server that serves many clients benefits from Ethernet, while a sensor project that occasionally sends data can use Wi‑Fi. Your takeaway: match the connection type to the project’s needs, and verify the assigned address after connecting so you can reach the Pi reliably. Wired vs Wireless on the Pi means use ethernet for reliability and servers; use wi‑fi for portability and convenience. verify interface names and ip assignment after connecting.. In practical terms, when to choose ethernet or wi‑fi and what each provides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choice guidance
keyIdea.text: Use Ethernet for reliability and servers; use Wi‑Fi for portability and convenience. Verify interface names and IP assignment after connecting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Wired vs Wireless
Why this comparison matters

Matching your connection type to a project reduces downtime and improves performance. Consider power, mobility, and expected traffic.

Key bullet points
  • Ethernet (eth0) typically delivers steady, low‑latency connectivity for servers.
  • Wi‑Fi (wlan0) offers mobility; performance depends on signal and congestion.
  • DHCP usually assigns a private IP; check it after connecting to locate the Pi.
  • Use Ethernet for long‑running services; use Wi‑Fi for portable or low‑traffic projects.
Side‑by‑side
Ethernet (eth0)
Stable, minimal interference, preferred for servers and Pi models with a gigabit port.
Wi‑Fi (wlan0)
Convenient for mobile setups; signal strength and network load affect performance.
Concrete example
For a home media server, plug the Pi into Ethernet to avoid stutters. For a field demo using a Pi Zero W, configure Wi‑Fi with saved credentials so it joins the event network automatically.
Key Takeaway

Pick Ethernet for reliability and Wi‑Fi for convenience; always verify the assigned IP after connecting.

screens.title: Find the Pi’s IP Address with the ip command
screens.subtitle: Identify eth0 and wlan0 and read the assigned address

narration.text: A fundamental skill is reading the Pi’s network addresses using the ip command. When you run the ip command with the address option it lists every interface and any assigned addresses. Look for typical interface names — eth0 for wired and wlan0 for wireless — and identify the IPv4 entry that looks like a private address such as one beginning with common home ranges. This tells you how other devices on the same network can reach the Pi. A practical example: after plugging in an Ethernet cable, run the ip command and look for eth0 to show inet followed by the address. If you see no address, the interface may not have negotiated with the router; try unplugging and replugging or check DHCP settings. A common misconception is that the hostname always resolves; on some networks you must use the numeric IP. After finding the address you should verify reachability with a connectivity test. Why this is useful: the numeric address is the direct way to open SSH sessions and VNC connections when name resolution fails. Find the Pi’s IP Address with the ip command means use the ip address command to confirm which interface has an assigned ip and copy that address for remote connections.. In practical terms, identify eth0 and wlan0 and read the assigned address. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IP lookup
keyIdea.text: Use the ip address command to confirm which interface has an assigned IP and copy that address for remote connections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Find the IP Address
Command overview
Run the ip address command to list interfaces and addresses. Find eth0 or wlan0 and read the inet entry for the IPv4 address assigned by DHCP.
Example output
3: wlan0: <…>
inet 192.168.1.45/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic wlan0
2: eth0: <…>
inet 192.168.1.12/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic eth0
Quick check
If no inet appears, DHCP did not assign an address. Try restarting networking or replugging the cable, or configure a static address for special setups.
Common mistake & fix
Assuming the hostname resolves. If the name does not resolve, use the numeric IP to connect. Also avoid trusting an IP without verifying reachability with a simple connectivity test.
Concrete task
On your Pi run the ip address command, note the inet address for the active interface, and write it down to use for SSH or VNC.
Key Takeaway

The numeric IP is the reliable handle for remote connections when name resolution is unavailable or unreliable.

screens.title: Verify Connectivity with ping
screens.subtitle: Confirm the Pi can reach other hosts and measure latency

narration.text: Verifying network connectivity is a short but vital diagnostic step. The ping tool sends small packets to a named host and reports the response time. If you can successfully ping a stable public host, your Pi has at least basic internet reachability. Use this to confirm both local and external connectivity: ping your router to check the local link, and ping a well known host to check outbound access. For example, pinging a widely available domain will show response times in milliseconds; press the interrupt key to stop the test. A common misconception is that a successful ping guarantees all services work; it only confirms basic IP reachability and a responsive host. If ping fails, check that the Pi has a valid IP address, that your local firewall or router allows ICMP traffic, and that the physical connection is present. This quick test should be part of your troubleshooting routine before attempting an SSH connection or file transfer. Verify Connectivity with ping means use ping to confirm local and external reachability; treat it as a preliminary check before remote sessions or transfers.. In practical terms, confirm the pi can reach other hosts and measure latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Connectivity test
keyIdea.text: Use ping to confirm local and external reachability; treat it as a preliminary check before remote sessions or transfers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Verify Connectivity
What ping tells you

Ping confirms that IP packets reach a host and that responses return. It reports latency and loss, but it does not test higher-level services like SSH.

Use cases
  • Ping the router to confirm local link is up.
  • Ping a public host to check internet access.
  • Use the result to gauge latency for time-sensitive tasks.
Concrete scenario
If SSH fails, ping the Pi from another device to verify it is reachable. If ping shows high loss or no replies, investigate the interface or router rather than assuming SSH is misconfigured.
Common mistake

A successful ping does not guarantee SSH or VNC access. Use ping as a first check, then test the specific service you need.

screens.title: SSH: Secure Shell Basics
screens.subtitle: What SSH provides and why it’s the default for headless Pi access

narration.text: Secure Shell, or SSH, provides an encrypted command‑line connection between your computer and the Raspberry Pi. It protects the login session and any commands you run, so credentials and data are not sent in plain text across the network. On a local network you can often connect using the Pi’s mDNS hostname, which looks like a name ending with the local domain; that works when mDNS is enabled on both devices. If name resolution fails, use the numeric IP address you found earlier. A simple example: use SSH from a laptop to run updates or manage files on a headless Pi without needing a monitor. A common misconception is that SSH is complicated to set up; modern Raspberry Pi OS enables the server easily and connecting from another device requires only a username and the host address. For improved security you will later replace password logins with SSH key pairs. The core claim: SSH gives you a secure, interactive terminal to operate the Pi remotely, and it’s the essential tool for headless workflows. SSH: Secure Shell Basics means ssh offers encrypted remote command-line access and is typically the primary way to manage a headless raspberry pi.. In practical terms, what ssh provides and why it’s the default for headless pi access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SSH value
keyIdea.text: SSH offers encrypted remote command-line access and is typically the primary way to manage a headless Raspberry Pi.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › SSH Basics
What SSH gives you
  • Encrypted terminal session to run commands remotely.
  • Secure channel for administration and scripting.
  • Works over local networks and, with care, across the internet.
Example
Open a secure shell from your laptop to the Pi to run package updates or inspect logs without a monitor attached to the Pi.
Hostname vs IP
On many home networks mDNS resolves names such as raspberrypi.local. If that fails, use the numeric IP you discovered. Name resolution is convenient but not guaranteed across every network.
Misconception

SSH is not only for advanced users; basic connections are simple and safe when you follow password or key guidance.

Takeaway: SSH is the efficient, encrypted way to manage a headless Pi and should be your first tool for remote command tasks.

screens.title: Connecting with SSH from Another Device
screens.subtitle: Steps to open a secure shell and common connection checks

narration.text: Connecting with SSH is a short sequence of checks and a single command. First, ensure the Pi is on the network and you have its IP address. Second, confirm the SSH service is enabled on the Pi; Raspberry Pi OS allows enabling it via configuration or a GUI. Third, from your client machine use the secure shell command with the target username and host. If the host key is new, your client will prompt you to accept it; this prevents man‑in‑the‑middle surprises. If a connection fails, verify that the Pi responds to ping, confirm the IP is correct, and ensure no firewall blocks port 22 on local devices. A typical beginner error is typing the hostname incorrectly; copy the address exactly. For stronger security, later convert to key‑based authentication and disable password logins. A concrete example: after confirming the IP, open a shell on your laptop, run the secure shell command to the Pi, accept the host key if asked, enter a password or use your local key, and then you will have a remote terminal to manage the Pi. What will you check first if the connection is refused?

keyIdea.title: SSH checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm network reachability and SSH is enabled, then connect and accept the host key. If refused, recheck IP, ping, and firewall settings.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Connect with SSH
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Confirm the Pi has an IP and responds to ping.
  2. 2. Ensure SSH is enabled on the Pi.
  3. 3. From your client run a secure shell command to the Pi’s user and host.
  4. 4. Accept the host key if prompted and authenticate.
Troubleshoot
If you see connection refused, check that the SSH service is running and that port 22 is not blocked by a firewall on the Pi or the network.
Concrete example
After noting 192.168.1.45 as the Pi’s IP, open a terminal on your laptop and use the secure shell command to connect as the Pi user. If the host key is new accept it, then authenticate and you will see the Pi’s shell prompt.
Key Takeaway

SSH is one command away but requires correct IP, an enabled service, and network reachability.

screens.title: Copy Files with scp
screens.subtitle: Securely move single files between your computer and the Pi

narration.text: Secure copy is the simplest way to transfer individual files to and from a Raspberry Pi. It uses the same secure channel as SSH, so credentials and file content are encrypted during transfer. Use scp when you need to copy a configuration file, a small log, or a single script. The basic pattern specifies the source and destination, including the remote username and host; when transferring to the Pi, provide the destination path on the Pi. A common beginner mistake is placing the destination dot in the wrong position or forgetting the username, which results in errors. For larger datasets or repeated transfers, scp will copy everything again and can be slower; in those cases prefer a synchronizing tool. A concrete example: copy a notes file from your laptop to the Pi’s home directory using scp and then log into the Pi to verify the file is present. After successful transfer, check the file owner and permissions to ensure the Pi user can read it. The main point: scp is secure and simple for one‑off file moves. Copy Files with scp means use scp for single file transfers over an encrypted channel; verify placement and permissions afterward.. In practical terms, securely move single files between your computer and the pi. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: scP use
keyIdea.text: Use scp for single file transfers over an encrypted channel; verify placement and permissions afterward.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Copy files with scp
When to use scp

Choose scp for simple, single-file transfers or a quick copy of a small asset to the Pi. It is encrypted and straightforward.

Example command
scp notes.txt pi@192.168.1.45:/home/pi/
After copying, verify the file exists on the Pi and check ownership and permissions so the intended user can read or execute it.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting the remote username or mistyping the host address.
  • Using scp for large directories — it will copy everything each time.
  • Ignoring permissions; files may be owned by root if copied with elevated privileges.
Key Takeaway

scp is secure and ideal for quick single-file transfers. For larger or repeated syncs use rsync instead.

screens.title: Efficient Transfers with rsync
screens.subtitle: When rsync saves time and bandwidth compared to scp

narration.text: rsync is a synchronizing copy tool that transfers only changed files or changed parts of files, which makes it efficient for directories and repeated backups. Unlike a simple secure copy which re‑sends all files, rsync compares source and destination and sends only differences. This is useful when you maintain a project folder on your laptop and update it frequently — rsync minimizes network usage and speeds up subsequent transfers. A practical example: synchronize a projects directory from your laptop to the Pi and let rsync preserve permissions and timestamps while only sending modified files. A common misunderstanding is that rsync is only for experts; the default options provide a safe and practical starting point. For remote transfers rsync typically runs over SSH for encryption. After a sync, verify file presence and, if needed, check a small sample of files to confirm integrity. The takeaway: use rsync for directories and regular backups, and prefer scp for quick single files. Efficient Transfers with rsync means rsync transfers only changed data, saving time and bandwidth for directories and repeated updates; it commonly runs over ssh for security.. In practical terms, when rsync saves time and bandwidth compared to scp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: rsync advantage
keyIdea.text: rsync transfers only changed data, saving time and bandwidth for directories and repeated updates; it commonly runs over SSH for security.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › rsync for efficient sync
How rsync works

rsync inspects source and destination and transfers only changed files or file blocks. This reduces bandwidth for repeated transfers and is ideal for backups and project syncs.

Example command
rsync -avz projects/ pi@192.168.1.45:/home/pi/projects/
The options commonly used preserve attributes and compress data during transfer.
When to prefer rsync
  • Large directories updated incrementally.
  • Frequent backups where only small changes occur.
  • When you want to preserve timestamps, permissions, and ownership.
Key Takeaway

rsync reduces transfer time and bandwidth for directories by syncing only changes. Run it over SSH for encrypted transfers.

screens.title: VNC Remote Desktop Overview
screens.subtitle: Why and when to enable remote graphical access

narration.text: VNC provides a full graphical remote desktop so you can run GUI applications on the Raspberry Pi from another computer. It’s useful when you need to interact with graphical tools, assist someone on a Pi desktop, or troubleshoot GUI-only problems. Raspberry Pi OS supports RealVNC and you can enable it via the configuration tool. To use it, enable the server on the Pi and run a VNC viewer on your main machine, then connect using the Pi’s IP or hostname. A common misconception is that VNC replaces SSH; rather, it complements SSH by giving a GUI when needed, while SSH remains the efficient method for command tasks. Performance depends on network speed and latency, so prefer Ethernet for demanding graphical work. For security, run VNC over an encrypted tunnel or use the built‑in encryption the server provides and restrict access to trusted hosts. The main idea: VNC adds a visual interface for tasks that benefit from a desktop, but apply the same network and security checks you used for SSH. VNC Remote Desktop Overview means use vnc when gui interaction is required; enable the server on the pi and connect with a viewer while following security best practices.. In practical terms, why and when to enable remote graphical access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: VNC purpose
keyIdea.text: Use VNC when GUI interaction is required; enable the server on the Pi and connect with a viewer while following security best practices.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › VNC Remote Desktop
When to use VNC
  • Run GUI applications remotely.
  • Assist another user by viewing and controlling their desktop.
  • Troubleshoot display or configuration issues without a physical monitor.
Note
Graphical sessions are sensitive to network latency; for best experience use wired connections when possible.
Concrete steps
Enable VNC via the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool or configuration utility. Install a compatible VNC viewer on your computer, then connect using the Pi’s address.
Common misconception

VNC is not always the fastest way to copy files or run commands; remain comfortable using SSH for those tasks and use VNC when a GUI is necessary.

screens.title: Enable VNC and Connect with a Viewer
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: enable the server, run a viewer, and authenticate

narration.text: To enable VNC on a Raspberry Pi start by enabling the server in the configuration utility or Raspberry Pi Configuration GUI. Once enabled, install and open a compatible VNC viewer on your main computer. Use the Pi’s IP address or mDNS hostname to connect and authenticate with the account you created on the Pi. If the Pi prompts for permission to accept a new viewer, agree and continue. Performance will be better on wired connections and may be slower over congested Wi‑Fi. A frequent oversight is forgetting to enable VNC or not installing a viewer on the client machine. If a connection fails, verify the Pi’s IP, ensure the VNC service is running, and confirm no firewall is blocking the VNC port. For security, prefer a viewer that supports encryption or tunnel the connection over SSH. After you connect, test a simple GUI application such as a file manager and confirm you can transfer clipboard text if needed. The final question to try: can you open a graphical text editor and save a file to the Pi’s home directory over VNC?

keyIdea.title: VNC steps
keyIdea.text: Enable the VNC server on the Pi, run a viewer on your computer, authenticate, and verify GUI interaction; prefer wired links and encrypted viewers when possible.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Enable VNC
Quick enable flow
  1. Open Raspberry Pi Configuration or run the configuration utility.
  2. Enable the VNC server and confirm the service is active.
  3. On your computer, open a VNC viewer and enter the Pi’s IP or hostname.
  4. Authenticate and accept any security prompts to start the session.
Troubleshooting
If the viewer cannot connect, verify the Pi’s IP, ensure VNC is running, and check local firewall rules. Consider tunneling VNC over SSH if direct connections are blocked.
Concrete task
Enable VNC on the Pi, install a viewer on your computer, connect, open a small GUI app, and save a file to confirm write access.
Key Takeaway

VNC gives useful GUI access; verify the service and network reachability and prefer encrypted viewers or SSH tunnels for security.

screens.title: Network Security Basics for the Pi
screens.subtitle: Simple practices that make a large difference

narration.text: When you place a Raspberry Pi on a network, basic security practices significantly reduce the risk of unauthorized access. Start by changing the default password and, when possible, disable password-based SSH logins in favor of SSH key pairs; keys are harder to brute force and are the recommended approach for administrative access. Keep the OS updated using the package update and upgrade sequence to receive security patches. Disable services you do not need — every exposed service is a potential entry point. Avoid exposing SSH directly to the public internet unless you protect it with a firewall, port controls, or a VPN. A common misconception is that a Pi on a home network is automatically safe; network devices can be discovered and targeted, so enforce good practices. For concrete steps: change the default password immediately, generate an SSH key pair on your client and copy the public key to the Pi, and regularly run updates. The core insight: simple, repeatable actions protect the device far more than leaving defaults in place. Practical security steps
  • Change the default password immediately after setup.
  • Use SSH key pairs and disable password authentication when practical.
  • Keep the system updated with package updates and upgrades.
  • Disable services you don’t need and restrict access to trusted hosts.
Concrete example
Generate a key pair on your laptop, copy the public key to the Pi’s authorized keys location, then disable password logins in the SSH server configuration. Test the key access before disabling passwords to avoid lockout.
Warning

Do not disable password logins before confirming your key access; losing remote access can require physical intervention.

Key Takeaway

Small, careful steps like keys and updates greatly reduce security risk compared to leaving defaults unchanged.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the compact ideas to carry forward. First, interface names like eth0 and wlan0 map to wired and wireless hardware; always confirm the inet address assigned by DHCP with the ip command. Second, SSH gives an encrypted shell and is the default tool for managing a headless Pi; rely on it for command tasks and use SSH keys for stronger authentication. Third, scp copies single files securely while rsync synchronizes directories efficiently by transferring only changes. Fourth, VNC provides a remote graphical desktop when you need GUI applications; enable the server and use a viewer while keeping performance and security in mind. Finally, apply basic security measures: change defaults, update the OS, restrict services, and avoid exposing SSH directly to the internet without extra protections. These concise points form the mental checklist you should apply whenever you put a new Pi on the network.
